My mother, who had grown up beside a lake and could not remember not knowing how, finally signed me up for adult lessons at the municipal pool, where nobody I knew would see me holding a kickboard.

[2] The instructor was a retired lifeguard named Mr. Osei, and his first lesson had nothing to do with strokes. He asked each of us to put our faces in the water and blow bubbles until they ran out of breath. [A] Most of the class managed it on the first try. I lasted about two seconds before I stood up, gasping, certain I had nearly bit the dust in three feet of water. [B] Mr. Osei did not laugh. He told me that the body's panic at having it's face covered is older than any of us, and that the only cure for it was repetition. [C] Every evening that week I filled the bathroom sink, set a timer, and put my face in until the beeping told me I could stop. [D]

[3] By the second lesson I could float on my back, an achievement that felt more like surrender than skill. Floating, it turned out, asked nothing of me except that I stop fighting the water. The strokes came slowly after that. My arms, which had spent fourteen years pulling doors and carrying groceries, was not used to pulling something that gave way. I swallowed a great deal of the pool.

[4] The test at the end of the course was a single length of the deep end. I remember the moment the floor dropped away beneath me and the water turned from pale green to a blue that seemed to go down forever and never end. My hand hit the far wall at last. Breathing hard, Mr. Osei wrote something on his clipboard while I hung there, and then he nodded once.

[5] I still am not a graceful swimmer. Even so, I know the difference between fear and danger now, and that the two are not always in the same place. The pool taught me that, it was never trying to hurt me, it was only waiting for me to stop thrashing.

passage_title: When the Lake Was a Crop
passage:
[1] For about sixty winters, from the 1850s until the First World War, the largest employer in the town of Millbrook was the lake itself. Each January, when the ice reached a thickness of twelve inches, crews of two hundred men and forty horses moved onto it and began cutting. Ice was the towns crop, and like any crop it had a season, a market, and it was priced.

[2] First a team scraped the snow off a field of ice the size of several city blocks. [A] Then a horse-drawn marker scored the surface into a grid of squares, each about twenty-two inches on a side. [B] Men with long saws cut along the lines, and the freed blocks, weighing more than two hundred pounds apiece, was floated down open channels to the icehouse on the shore. [C] There they were hauled up a ramp by a steam-powered conveyor and stacked in layers separated by sawdust, which kept them so well that ice cut in February was still being shipped in August. [D]

[3] Most of it went by rail to the city, seventy miles south, where it was used for the purpose of cooling the iceboxes of hotels and restaurants and the holds of fish dealers. The finest blocks, clear enough to read a newspaper through, were sold at a premium. Cloudy ice, which had frozen with air trapped in it, went to the breweries at half the price.

[4] The trade shaped the town in ways that outlasted it. The rail spur that once carried ice now carries commuters. The icehouse foundations, too solid to remove, became the base of the public boathouse. Even the street names remember the trade: Sawdust Lane runs along the old shore, and Marker Street follows the line where the horses were stabled.

[5] What ended it was not a warm winter but a machine. By 1910 mechanical refrigeration had become cheap enough for a hotel to make its own ice, within a decade the market for the natural kind had melted away. The last harvest on the lake took place in 1919. A photograph of it hangs in the town library: a few dozen men standing in a row on the ice, their saws held upright like rifles, looking as though they already knew they were the last.
